newsitem.title: USA: IPO HIGHLIGHTS-New issues climb out of brief hole.
newsitem.headline: IPO HIGHLIGHTS-New issues climb out of brief hole.

text.p: Initial public offerings found themselves with hardly a buyer in sight due to rough seas in the technology industry earlier this week, forcing underwriters to slash prices for new companies.

But IPO analysts says the fall-off is likely to be temporary after the Nasdaq's sharp rise on Wednesday and strong January cash inflows of $24 billion pouring into stock mutual funds, according to the Investment Company Institute.

"Everything just fell apart when technology shares fell apart. Demand for deals really loosened up. Deals that had looked like premiums -- Apex, DAOU, Radiant, Qualix -- it looks none of them would get a premium now," said Vince Slavin of Cantor Fitzgerald.
After demand slacked, underwriters had to slash prices.

DAOU Systems Inc, which makes computer networking systems for healthcare provider organizations, was expected to be a hot IPO. But yesterday the company cut its IPO down more than half from its initial expectations. The shares priced at 9 and climbed only 1/4 in their market debut today.

Contact lens company Wesley Jessen VisionCare Inc also dramatically cut the price for its shares, finally selling at $15 a share, a bargain-basement level compared to its first estimated price of $19 to $21. The shares rose 1-1/4 to 16-1/4 in their market debut today.

Software company Qualix Group Inc first estimated shares would price between $9 and $11 but shares were sold for less, $8 each. They rose on their first day of trading Wednesday to 9-1/4, still in the low end of their original expectations.
Radiant Systems Inc shares priced low but posted a somewhat better first day gain. Its shares opened at 11-1/4, up from their IPO price of $9.50 a share.

"After the volatility in the Nasdaq we started to look again at what was going on in new issues. It got a little noisier, but unless the trend continues, it shouldn't (be seen as a slump)," said Mitch Whiteford of Robertson Stephens & Co.

David Menlow, president of the IPO Financial Network, said the revisions were a reflection of the strong current of selectivity in the IPO market and were more indicative of the specific companies at bat to go public this week than a general market trend.

"There's just an intolerance in the marketplace for deals that are not priced right or deals of a mediocre substance. And underwriters don't want their deals to break so they are getting priced more cheaply," he said.
